CAR WASH EMPLOYER REGISTRATION, BONDING, AND SUCCESSOR LIABILITY (LABOR CODE §§ 2050–2066) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Car Wash, LLC

ABOUT THIS CAR WASH EMPLOYER REGISTRATION INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's regulation of the car washing and polishing industry under Labor Code Part 8.5 (Sections 2050 through 2068), added in 2003: the annual registration every covered car wash employer files with the Labor Commissioner, the $150,000 surety bond and workers' compensation documentation that registration depends on, the sworn application and its disclosure items, the grounds on which registration or renewal is unavailable, the fees and the Car Wash Worker Restitution Fund, the posting and three-year recordkeeping duties, the daily civil fine for operating unregistered, and the statutory successor liability that can follow a predecessor's unpaid wages onto a later operator at the same site. Acme Car Wash, LLC is considering engaging Jordan T. Reyes in connection with the position of Car wash attendant in work that this Part may cover.

This corpus separately includes a Property Service Workers Protection Act: Janitorial Employer Registration — Information Sheet, a Farm Labor Contractor Licensing — Information Sheet, and a Garment Manufacturing Registration and Brand Guarantor Wage Liability — Information Sheet, each describing a different industry-specific registration scheme with its own definitions, bond or guarantee provisions, and penalties. It also separately includes a Successor Liability When Buying a Business's Assets — Information Sheet, which covers the general corporate successorship rules of Ray v. Alad Corp. that the car wash statute's own successor provision has been held not to incorporate, and a Tip Pooling and Gratuities Ownership — Information Sheet addressing the gratuities sections the car wash bond is written to secure. This document does not determine whether Acme Car Wash, LLC's or Jordan T. Reyes's activities meet the statutory definitions of “car washing and polishing,” “employer,” or “employee,” whether any statutory exclusion applies, or whether any registration, bond, recordkeeping, or successor-liability provision applies to any specific person or entity.

“CAR WASHING AND POLISHING,” “EMPLOYER,” AND “EMPLOYEE” DEFINED
Labor Code Part 8.5, added in 2003, regulates the car washing and polishing industry. Section 2051 supplies the definitions that decide who the Part reaches. “Car washing and polishing” covers washing, cleaning, drying, polishing, detailing, servicing, or otherwise providing cosmetic care to vehicles, and expressly does not include motor vehicle repair as defined in Business and Professions Code Section 9880.1. An “employer” is any individual, partnership, corporation, limited liability company, joint venture, or association engaged in that business that engages any other individual to provide those services. The definition of “employee” is written broadly: it reaches any person who renders actual car washing and polishing services for an employer, states expressly that a minor or a person who is not a citizen or national of the United States is included, and applies whether the person is paid in tips or wages and whether the pay is calculated by time, piece, task, commission, or another method.

BUSINESSES EXCLUDED FROM THE DEFINITION OF “EMPLOYER”
Section 2051(b)(2) removes several categories of business from the definition of “employer,” so that the Part's registration and bonding scheme does not reach them. The excluded categories are a charitable, youth, service, veteran, or sports group, club, or association that washes cars on an intermittent basis to raise funds for charitable, education, or religious purposes; a licensed vehicle dealer or car rental agency whose car washing is ancillary to its primary business of selling, leasing, or servicing vehicles; a new motor vehicle dealer as defined in Vehicle Code Section 426 that is primarily engaged in selling, leasing, renting, or servicing vehicles; an automotive repair dealer as defined in Business and Professions Code Section 9880.1(a) primarily engaged in repairing and diagnosing motor vehicle malfunctions; and a self-service or automated car wash whose employees are for cashiering or maintenance purposes only.

ANNUAL REGISTRATION WITH THE LABOR COMMISSIONER AND THE BAR ON OPERATING WITHOUT IT
Section 2054 states the core duty in a single sentence: every employer within the meaning of the Part registers with the Labor Commissioner annually. Section 2060 states the corresponding prohibition — no employer may conduct any business without complying with both the registration and the bond requirements of the registration chapter. The Part itself is framed as an exercise of the state's police power, and Section 2050 states that the civil penalties the chapter provides are in addition to any other penalty provided by law.

CONDITIONS THE LABOR COMMISSIONER REQUIRES BEFORE REGISTRATION OR RENEWAL
Section 2055 lists what must be in place before the Labor Commissioner may permit an employer to register or to renew a registration. The employer must have applied by presenting proof of compliance with the local government's business licensing or regional regulatory requirements; must have obtained the surety bond the same section requires, which a separate clause of this document addresses; must have documented that a current workers' compensation insurance policy is in effect for the employees; and must have paid the fees established under Section 2059.

THE $150,000 SURETY BOND, ITS BENEFICIARIES, AND THE COLLECTIVE BARGAINING EXCEPTION
Section 2055(b) conditions registration on a surety bond issued by a surety company admitted to do business in California, in a principal sum of not less than $150,000, a copy of which the employer files with the Labor Commissioner. The bond runs in favor of and is payable to the people of the State of California, and it is for the benefit of any employee damaged by the employer's failure to pay wages, interest on wages, or fringe benefits, or damaged by a violation of Labor Code Section 351 or 353, the gratuities provisions. A surety must give the employer and the commissioner 30 days' written notice before cancelling or terminating the bond, and the statute states that an employer shall not conduct any business until it obtains a new bond and files a copy with the commissioner. The bond subdivision does not apply to an employer covered by a valid collective bargaining agreement that expressly provides for wages, hours of work, working conditions, and an expeditious process to resolve disputes concerning nonpayment of wages.

THE SWORN WRITTEN APPLICATION AND ITS REQUIRED DISCLOSURES
Section 2061 conditions approval of a registration on a written application, in a form the Labor Commissioner prescribes, subscribed and sworn by the employer. The application asks for business-entity identification, incorporation details, federal and state employer identification numbers, business and branch addresses, and whether the filing is a new or renewal registration. It also asks for the names, residential addresses, telephone numbers, and Social Security numbers of corporate officers, of all persons exercising management responsibility, and of all persons — other than bona fide employees on regular salaries — holding a financial interest of 10 percent or more, along with each such person's percentage. Two disclosure items look backward at the applicant's own compliance history: whether any of those persons presently owes unpaid wages, has unpaid judgments outstanding, has liens or suits pending, or owes payroll or income taxes, Social Security taxes, or disability insurance; and whether any of them has ever been cited or assessed a penalty for violating any provision of the Labor Code. An affirmative answer triggers a duty to supply additional detail, including, for citations, the date, nature, penalty amount, disposition, and any appeal.

CIRCUMSTANCES IN WHICH REGISTRATION OR RENEWAL IS UNAVAILABLE
Section 2062 bars the Labor Commissioner from registering or renewing the registration of an employer in three circumstances: the employer has not fully satisfied a final judgment for unpaid wages due to an employee or former employee of a business for which registration is required; the employer has failed to remit the proper amount of contributions required by the Unemployment Insurance Code, or the Employment Development Department has made a final assessment for unpaid contributions that the employer has not fully paid; or the employer has failed to remit Social Security and Medicare tax contributions required by the Federal Insurance Contributions Act and has not fully paid that delinquency.

REGISTRATION FEES AND THE CAR WASH WORKER RESTITUTION FUND
Section 2059 directs the Labor Commissioner to collect a registration fee from employers for each branch location and permits periodic adjustment of that fee in an amount sufficient to fund the direct and indirect costs of administering and enforcing the Part, subject to a limit: the fee may not be increased unless the published fund balance is projected to fall below 25 percent of annual expenditures. In addition, each employer is assessed an annual fee equal to 20 percent of the registration fee for each branch location, which is deposited in the Car Wash Worker Restitution Fund. Section 2065 establishes that fund in the State Treasury, funded by that annual fee, by 50 percent of the fines collected under Section 2064, and by an amount equal to 20 percent of the initial registration fee. Upon appropriation by the Legislature, the commissioner disburses the fund only to persons the commissioner determines were damaged by an employer's failure to pay wages, penalties, and other damages, and the statute states that those disbursements are made to ensure payment of amounts determined due to a car wash worker as a result of a violation of the Labor Code by a registered or unregistered car wash business.

PROOF OF REGISTRATION, WORKPLACE POSTING, AND THE RENEWAL NOTICE
Section 2057 states that proof of registration is an official Division of Labor Standards Enforcement registration form, and that each employer posts that form where employees may read it during the workday. Section 2056 directs the commissioner, when a certificate of registration is first issued or renewed, to provide the registrant with related and supplemental information about business administration and applicable labor laws. Section 2058 directs the commissioner to mail a renewal notice to the registrant's last known address at least 30 days before the registration expires, but states that the commissioner's omission to send that notice does not excuse a registrant from applying for renewal on time, is not a defense in any action or proceeding involving failure to renew, and does not subject the commissioner to legal liability.

THREE-YEAR RECORDKEEPING DUTY

In People ex rel. Harris v. Alad Corp. or the workers' compensation successorship test of Superior Care Facilities. The business held liable there had not bought anything from the predecessor: the predecessor car wash was evicted after a foreclosure, and the new operator leased the same premises from the new owner and ran a car wash there. Because it used substantially the same facilities to offer substantially the same services, it fell within subdivision (a). The court also rejected a due process objection based on lack of notice of the predecessor's wage debts, reasoning that Section 2066 itself supplies notice of the potential for successor liability to anyone entering the industry. One justice dissented, reading the statute to require that the defendant actually succeed to the predecessor's business before the four criteria come into play. The California Supreme Court denied review on July 25, 2012.

expectedJSON.body: Section 2059 directs the Labor Commissioner to collect a registration fee from employers for each branch location and permits periodic adjustment of that fee in an amount sufficient to fund the direct and indirect costs of administering and enforcing the Part, subject to a limit: the fee may not be increased unless the published fund balance is projected to fall below 25 percent of annual expenditures. In addition, each employer is assessed an annual fee equal to 20 percent of the registration fee for each branch location, which is deposited in the Car Wash Worker Restitution Fund. Section 2065 establishes that fund in the State Treasury, funded by that annual fee, by 50 percent of the fines collected under Section 2064, and by an amount equal to 20 percent of the initial registration fee. Upon appropriation by the Legislature, the commissioner disburses the fund only to persons the commissioner determines were damaged by an employer's failure to pay wages, penalties, and other damages, and the statute states that those disbursements are made to ensure payment of amounts determined due to a car wash worker as a result of a violation of the Labor Code by a registered or unregistered car wash business.

expectedJSON.body: Section 2066 makes a successor to a car wash employer that owed wages and penalties to the predecessor's former employees liable for those wages and penalties if the successor meets any one of four criteria: it uses substantially the same facilities or workforce to offer substantially the same services as the predecessor; it shares in the ownership, management, control of labor relations, or interrelations of business operations with the predecessor; it employs in a managerial capacity any person who directly or indirectly controlled the wages, hours, or working conditions of the predecessor's affected employees; or it is an immediate family member of any owner, partner, officer, or director of the predecessor employer of any person who had a financial interest in the predecessor employer. The criteria are stated in the disjunctive — meeting any one of them suffices.

expectedJSON.body: In People ex rel. Harris v. Sunset Car Wash, LLC (2012) 205 Cal.App.4th 1433, the Second District Court of Appeal held that the four circumstances listed in Section 2066 themselves define who is a “successor,” so that a court need not import definitions of successorship from other bodies of law such as the corporate asset-purchase rule of Ray v. Alad Corp. or the workers' compensation successorship test of Superior Care Facilities. The business held liable there had not bought anything from the predecessor: the predecessor car wash was evicted after a foreclosure, and the new operator leased the same premises from the new owner and ran a car wash there. Because it used substantially the same facilities to offer substantially the same services, it fell within subdivision (a). The court also rejected a due process objection based on lack of notice of the predecessor's wage debts, reasoning that Section 2066 itself supplies notice of the potential for successor liability to anyone entering the industry. One justice dissented, reading the statute to require that the defendant actually succeed to the predecessor's business before the four criteria come into play. The California Supreme Court denied review on July 25, 2012.
